VICO SOTTO PUSHES ANTI-POLITICAL DYNASTY BILL

WATCH: Pasig Mayor Vico Sotto calls for the passage of a law banning political dynasties during a consultative meeting led by Senator Risa Hontiveros in Pasig City. 

“Hindi ito tungkol sa kahit sinong indibidwal o spesipikong pamilya… What we are against here is the concentration of power in the hands of a few political elite,” Sotto said. 

He stressed the need to level the playing field and prevent state resources from being used to perpetuate political families in power. 

“Sa sitwasyon natin sa Pilipinas, nine times out of ten, ang nananalo ay miyembro ng political family,” he added. 

Sotto hopes Congress “will really be serious” about passing the anti-political dynasty bill now and urged civil society organizations to rally support for the measure. | @eimorpsantos

Why the Taiwan Strait matters: Rerouting is possible, but costly- featuring Japan, South Korea, Australia, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia

If traffic through the Taiwan Strait is disrupted, shipping does not stop, but every alternative comes with trade-offs

Via the Luzon Strait (east of Taiwan) A container ship can bypass the Taiwan Strait by sailing through the Luzon Strait and east of Taiwan.
* Distance impact: relatively limited
* Operational impact: likely skips Chinese port calls
Implication: even a “short” detour can disconnect China from key legs of regional supply chains.

Avoiding Taiwan altogether (south of the Philippines >> Miyako Strait) From Singapore, a more cautious route runs south of the Philippines, then north through the Miyako Strait to reach Korea/Japan.
* Distance impact: roughly +1,000 miles
* Cost & time: materially higher fuel costs and delays
* Ports: stopping at Chinese ports becomes infeasible en route to Busan
* Ripple effects: significant, given China’s central role in maritime shipping.

Who depends most on the Taiwan Strait
Japan & South Korea
Both countries sit high on imports and exports routed through the Taiwan Strait, reflecting deep integration with Northeast Asian supply chains. Their exposure is two-sided: disruption hits inputs and outputs simultaneously.

Australia
Australia shows moderate reliance, lower than Northeast Asia but still meaningful. Disruptions translate into longer routes and higher costs, especially for time-sensitive goods.

Africa & the Middle East (Specifically UAE and Saudi Aaabia)

A striking contrast appears here:
The large blue marker on the left represents the UAE, indicating lower export reliance on the Taiwan Strait, consistent with diversified routes and hub-based logistics.

The large marker on the right represents Saudi Arabia, showing much higher export exposure via the Taiwan Strait.

Interpretation: even within the same region, trade structure and routing choices create very different risk profiles.

So...
Rerouting around the Taiwan Strait is possible, but not neutral. Each alternative raises distance, costs, delays, and foregone port calls, reshaping supply chains in ways that matter for producers—,, and prices consumers pay. The charts together show who is most exposed, and the map explains why that exposure quickly becomes expensive.

Source: @CSIS @ChinaPowerCSIS by Matthew P. Funaiole, Brian Hart, David Peng, Bonny Lin, and Jasper Verschuur,  Jaehyun Han
More credit: Michael Kohler, Fabio Murgia, Mariel de la Garza, Katherine Stark, Leon Li, Samantha Lu, Aidan Powers-Riggs, and Truly Tinsley.

🇯🇵 The High-Stakes Gamble of Takaichi: A Landslide Victory and Its Implications for East Asia⚠️

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s decision to dissolve parliament and call a snap election—followed by a crushing victory—was not merely a domestic political episode. It was the successful validation of a high-risk political strategy, jointly endorsed by voters and institutions. That outcome is now reshaping Japan’s national trajectory and generating spillover risks across the region.

🔄First, Japan has entered a phase of security-led state reconstruction. With a supermajority secured, constitutional revision is no longer a question of political courage but of sequencing and technique. Through reinterpretation, supplementary clauses, and policy implementation, the postwar constitutional constraints will be steadily eroded. Military capability development is no longer confined to defensive purposes; it is increasingly framed as a tool for shaping regional order. Nuclear armament will not be openly declared, but its technical preparedness and normative taboos are being systematically relaxed.

🚨Second, Takaichi’s landslide does not point toward stabilization in Sino–Japanese relations. A prevailing view among Japan’s right wing holds that decisive electoral strength will compel China to “recognize reality” and seek accommodation. This misreads Beijing’s strategic logic. From China’s perspective, Takaichi’s victory is not a diplomatic signal but proof that a Taiwan-centered, anti-China security narrative can deliver decisive electoral returns. The rational response, therefore, is not adaptation but cost escalation—to prevent this political model from becoming replicable elsewhere. As a result, bilateral relations are likely to shift toward a more prolonged, instrumentalized, and cost-explicit confrontation, rather than a stable but tense equilibrium.

💴Third, Japan’s economy and financial system are becoming central arenas of strategic pressure. The risk does not stem solely from rising defense spending. Japan enters this phase with high public debt, weak growth, and severely constrained monetary policy. Under such conditions, sensitivity to external shocks is acute. China retains leverage across rare earths, critical materials, industrial access, and financial expectation management—for example, through selective tightening in key mineral supply chains or calibrated signaling that reshapes expectations toward yen-denominated assets. These tools need not be deployed openly to be effective; over time, they can erode Japan’s strategic resilience without overt confrontation.

📱Fourth, Takaichi’s victory signals a structural shift in Japanese electoral politics. Digital mobilization, identity polarization, and security anxiety have proven electorally efficient. This will compress the space for technocratic governance, sharpen policy positions, and raise political risk tolerance across the system.

The most consequential uncertainty lies beyond Japan itself. Takaichi’s success offers a clear template: anti-China framing combined with security anxiety and digital populism. This model may be rapidly emulated across Europe’s periphery, middle powers in Asia, and parts of Latin America. Whether this path travels will define the next phase. The Philippines stands out as a critical test case—where replication or rejection will determine whether this political strategy becomes transnational.

Takaichi’s landslide was not a beginning, but a confirmation: high-risk politics has now been proven winnable.

#Takaichi #高市早苗 #JapanElection #Geopolitics #EastAsia #ChinaJapan
